blocks.title: Which one
blocks.text: JSON-in-a-string wins when you always read the whole object. A hash wins when fields are updated independently or read selectively.

lines: # 1M flags as 1M top-level keys: ~80 MB overhead

items: `listpack` while under 128 entries and 64-byte values
`hashtable` above either threshold
Every top-level key costs ~50–90 bytes before your data
robj + dict entry + expire entry + key string
Hashes amortize that overhead across all their fields

blocks.title: Limits and mistakes
items: Fields cannot nest; values are always strings
No independent type beyond the field TTL
`HGETALL` on a 100k-field bucket ships megabytes
That one command stalls the event loop
`HMSET` deprecated — variadic `HSET` replaces it
`HINCRBY`/`HINCRBYFLOAT`: atomic per-field counters
A whole stats object in one key, no read-modify-write race
`HKEYS`/`HVALS`/`HGETALL` are all O(N) — use `HSCAN`
`HRANDFIELD key [count] [WITHVALUES]` samples fields
Negative count allows repeats, mirroring `SRANDMEMBER`

lines: HTTL user:1000 FIELDS 1 otp   # HPERSIST clears

blocks.title: Per-field TTL
blocks.text: `HEXPIRE`/`HPEXPIRE`/`HEXPIREAT` expire one field without touching the rest of the object. `HTTL` reads it, `HPERSIST` removes it.

items: Need uniqueness? Yes → set or sorted set. No → list or string
Need order? Insertion → list. Score → sorted set. None → set or hash
Address parts independently? Yes → hash. No → string
string: whole-value only, no partial reads
list: duplicates allowed, also a stack
set: unordered, unique, set algebra for free
sorted set: ordered by score, also a priority queue
hash: fields unordered, each independently writable

blocks.title: Commands that block
items: `KEYS`, `SMEMBERS`, `HGETALL`
`LRANGE 0 -1`, `ZRANGE 0 -1`, `SORT`
`DEL` on a huge collection
`FLUSHALL` without `ASYNC`

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Any command whose result size grows with the collection needs a `LIMIT`/`COUNT` bound or a `*SCAN` cursor. "Fast" means "bounded N".

items: Same data, three shapes — pick by what you must query
Small collections are dramatically cheaper per element
Big-O is per command; latency is per server
O(N) with N = 10^6 is milliseconds of blocking for everyone

blocks.title: Counter-example
blocks.text: Compact encodings are linear-scan. A `listpack` hash of 500 fields is slower per lookup than a `hashtable`. The thresholds exist for a reason.

items: streams: append-only logs with consumer groups
geospatial (sorted-set-backed): radius queries
JSON module: nested documents
Search module: secondary indexes

lines: SADD visitors:0907 u9   # exact, lists members
SETBIT active:0907 9 1  # exact, dense int IDs
PFCOUNT hll:0907        # PFMERGE rolls up weeks

items: Pick HLL when you only need "how many unique?"
Never need to list or test members — HLL cannot do either
`SCARD` is exact but stores every element forever
Bitmap is sized by max ID, not by member count
Sparse IDs make a bitmap wasteful; dense IDs make it tiny

blocks.title: PFCOUNT gotcha
blocks.text: `PFCOUNT` on one key is O(1) but caches its estimate in the key — it is a write command and fails on a read-only replica.

left.title: pipeline
items: N commands, 1 RTT
not atomic
throughput lever
others interleave

right.title: MULTI/EXEC
items: queued then serial
nothing interleaves
no rollback
still one RTT
Pipelining sends N commands without waiting for replies
Biggest throughput lever there is, and it is not atomic
`MULTI` queues, `EXEC` runs them with nothing interleaved
A runtime error in one queued command does not undo the rest

lines: EXEC   # nil if cart:42 changed -> retry

items: `EVAL script numkeys key ... arg ...` runs atomically
`SCRIPT LOAD` then `EVALSHA` to skip resending the body
Use for read-then-write logic that must not interleave
`FUNCTION LOAD` + `FCALL` is the modern persisted replacement
Keep scripts short — slow Lua blocks the server like any command

blocks.title: Lock release
blocks.text: Acquire with `SET lock:<res> <token> NX EX 30`. Release must be that Lua compare-and-delete, or you will delete somebody else's lock.

items: Keys are removed lazily on access, plus an active sampling cycle
An expired key can hold memory a while after its TTL passes
Only top-level keys expire, aside from hash-field TTLs
No expiring one list element or one set member
Model that as a sorted set scored by time + `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`
`EXPIRE key 60`, `TTL key`, `PERSIST key` removes it
`TTL` returns -1 for no TTL, -2 for no key at all
`SET` replaces the value and clears the TTL with it
`APPEND`, `LPUSH`, `HSET`, `INCR` mutate in place and keep it
`SET key v KEEPTTL` preserves the TTL through a replace

blocks.title: Deleting safely
items: `DEL key` is O(N) in elements freed
`UNLINK key` frees in a background thread
`UNLINK` returns immediately — prefer it on big keys
Cache-aside: `GET`, on miss load DB, `SET key val EX ttl`
Add random jitter to the TTL so the herd does not expire together
`notify-keyspace-events` publishes expirations and evictions
Delivery is fire-and-forget — it is not a queue
`SCAN`/`SSCAN`/`HSCAN`/`ZSCAN` are the only safe walks in prod

blocks.title: maxmemory policies
items: `noeviction`: writes fail with `OOM command not allowed`
`allkeys-lru` / `allkeys-lfu`: evict anything
`volatile-ttl`: evict the soonest to expire
Choose deliberately — the default surprises people
Big keys: millions of elements make every touch slow
They block failover and cannot be sharded
`KEYS *` in app code — the classic production stall
Unbounded growth: no `LTRIM`, no `ZREMRANGEBYRANK`, no TTL
No TTL on cache keys: they never leave, writes fail at `maxmemory`
Wrong type: `LINDEX` in a loop, `SMEMBERS` then client-side filter
Wrong type: a JSON string rewritten for one field change
N+1 round trips: N sequential `GET`s = N network RTTs
Fix with `MGET`, a pipeline, or one Lua script

blocks.title: Cluster gotcha
blocks.text: Multi-key commands (`SINTER`, `MGET`, `ZUNIONSTORE`) need every key in the same hash slot. Force it with a hash tag: `{user1000}:profile`.

items: `SLOWLOG GET` lists commands over `slowlog-log-slower-than`
First place to look when latency spikes
`OBJECT ENCODING key` confirms the compact encoding held
`MONITOR` streams every command — debugging only, it slows the server

blocks.title: The whole handbook
items: string: a byte array with a counter bolted on
list: a deque
set: membership and algebra
sorted set: an index you can rank
hash: an object with addressable fields

blocks.title: Mental model
blocks.text: Pick the type by access pattern, keep every N bounded, batch your round trips, and give every key a lifecycle. Everything else is detail.

caption.text: Part 2 of REDIS DATA TYPES. Most Redis outages are not Redis being slow — they are one O(N) command holding a single-threaded server hostage while 500 clients wait. This handbook walks all five core types: their internal encodings, the commands worth memorising, the Big-O of each, and the exact mistakes (KEYS *, SMEMBERS, HGETALL on a 100k-field bucket) that turn a cache into a stall. Ten pages, from the flat keyspace to SLOWLOG.
